learn.title: How Solar PV Panels Generate Electricity
learn.intro: Solar PV panels convert sunlight into electricity, a cornerstone of the global energy transition. Understanding their operation helps us harness renewable energy efficiently for homes, businesses, and utilities worldwide. This knowledge empowers communities to reduce carbon footprints and achieve energy independence.
learn.c1_text: When photons hit a solar cell, they knock electrons loose from atoms. This is the photoelectric effect, first observed by Einstein. Like a water wheel turning when water hits it, electrons flow when energized by light. Each photon transfers energy to free an electron, creating electric current.
learn.c2_text: Silicon wafers in PV cells have electrons that need a 'push' to flow. Doping adds impurities to create positive and negative layers. When light hits, electrons jump from the negative to positive layer, generating direct current. This process is similar to how batteries store chemical energy for later use.
learn.c3_text: India's solar capacity reached 90 GW in 2024, with rooftop installations expanding rapidly. The MNRE supports grid integration and manufacturing. Tamil Nadu leads with 17 GW installed, while Rajasthan hosts large solar parks. Each panel contributes to India's goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
learn.stat3: Silicon covers 95% of global PV market

learn.title: India's Solar Manufacturing PLI Scheme
learn.intro: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme accelerates India's solar manufacturing sector, crucial for energy security and export potential. By incentivizing local production, India aims to reduce import dependence and create jobs, aligning with its renewable energy ambitions under the National Solar Mission.
learn.c1_text: The MNRE's PLI scheme offers incentives for solar module manufacturing. Companies receive subsidies based on incremental sales over base levels. For every 10% sales growth, manufacturers get 25% of the incentive. This mirrors China's success in scaling solar production through similar policies.
learn.c2_text: Incentives range from 5-6% of incremental sales, capped at ₹15,000 crore. Eligible products include PV modules and components. The scheme targets 28 GW annual manufacturing capacity by 2026. Like tax credits in the US, it rewards output growth while ensuring quality standards.
learn.c3_text: India aims to manufacture 200 GW solar equipment by 2030. The PLI scheme supports 100 GW capacity with ₹15,000 crore incentives. Gujarat and Tamil Nadu lead in setting up plants. This aligns with India's 500 GW non-fossil target and Atmanirbhar Bharat self-reliance vision.

learn.title: Demand Response for Grid Balance
learn.intro: Demand response programs enable large energy consumers to adjust consumption, stabilizing grids with variable renewables. By reducing or shifting loads during peak times, industrial consumers help prevent blackouts while earning revenue. This flexible resource is vital for integrating wind and solar into power systems.
learn.c1_text: Large consumers adjust energy use based on grid needs. During high demand, they reduce consumption; during low demand, they increase it. Like traffic lights managing flow, DR optimizes supply-demand balance. The US DOE reports DR saves 2-5% of peak capacity nationally.
learn.c2_text: DR reduces the need for peaking power plants, which are expensive and polluting. It provides fast-acting reserves like virtual batteries. Smart meters and IoT enable real-time adjustments. California's DR program avoids 1,000 MW of fossil generation daily, equivalent to four gas plants.
learn.c3_text: India's discoms partner with industries for DR under UDAY. Gujarat leads with 1,200 MW DR capacity. Steel plants and cement factories participate by reducing loads during peak hours. The scheme saves ₹1.5 lakh crore annually, aligning with India's 500 GW renewable target by 2030.
learn.stat3: California saves 1,000 MW daily via DR
learn.stat4: US DR market valued at $10 billion

learn.title: Lithium-Ion Battery Storage Explained
learn.intro: Lithium-ion batteries store excess renewable energy for later use, solving intermittency challenges. Their efficiency and falling costs make them ideal for grid applications and electric vehicles. Understanding their operation unlocks opportunities for sustainable energy systems globally and in India's growing renewable sector.
learn.c1_text: Li-ion cells use lithium ions moving between cathode and anode. During discharge, lithium moves from anode to cathode, releasing electrons through the external circuit. Like a rechargeable flashlight, they store 150-250 Wh/kg. Tesla's Megapack stores 3.9 MWh per unit, enabling grid-scale storage.
learn.c2_text: Batteries provide frequency regulation, peak shaving, and renewable firming. They respond in milliseconds, unlike gas turbines. The Hornsdale Power Reserve in Australia uses 150 MW Tesla batteries, preventing blackouts. In India, batteries support solar microgrids in rural areas with 8-hour evening supply.
learn.c3_text: India's battery storage reached 10 GWh in 2024, with ₹10,000 crore incentives under NIESP. The Kurnool 100 MW project in Andhra Pradesh uses 100 MWh batteries. Startups like Exicom expand EV charging networks. BYD supplies batteries for 10,000 electric buses planned by 2030 under FAME II.

learn.title: Green Hydrogen via Water Electrolysis
learn.intro: Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water with renewable electricity, offers zero-emission fuel for hard-to-abate sectors. Comparing PEM and alkaline electrolyzers reveals trade-offs in efficiency, cost, and scalability. This technology is pivotal for decarbonizing steel, shipping, and heavy industry globally.
learn.c1_text: PEM electrolyzers use a polymer membrane, operating at 80°C with 70-80% efficiency. They start quickly but cost $1,200/kW. Alkaline systems use liquid KOH, run at 90°C, and cost $800/kW. Both produce hydrogen at 2-3 kg per MWh, but PEM suits variable renewable sources better.
learn.c2_text: PEM electrolyzers achieve 70-80% efficiency vs 60-70% for alkaline. They handle rapid power fluctuations, ideal for solar/wind integration. Hydrogen stores energy for weeks or months. IRENA notes green H2 could supply 10% of global energy by 2050, replacing gray hydrogen in ammonia production.
learn.c3_text: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MT production by 2030. Gujarat and Tamil Nadu host pilot projects using alkaline electrolyzers. The cost is $3-6/kg, dropping to $1.5/kg by 2030. IRENA supports partnerships for technology transfer, aligning with India's 500 GW renewable target.
learn.stat1: Global green H2 potential: 980 million tonnes/year
learn.stat3: India's target: 5 MT green H2 by 2030

learn.title: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.intro: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to produce clean hydrogen at scale, reducing fossil fuel dependence and creating green jobs. With $2.5 billion allocated, the mission targets 5 MT/year production by 2030, positioning India as a global green hydrogen exporter and aligning with climate commitments.
learn.c1_text: The mission aims for 5 million tonnes annual green hydrogen production by 2030. It includes ₹10,000 crore capital subsidy for pilot projects. Like the solar PLI scheme, it incentivizes manufacturing. The target supports India's 500 GW renewable energy goal and reduces oil import costs by $10 billion annually.
learn.c2_text: Capital subsidy of 60% for first 5 GW projects, decreasing to 30% later. Tariff support at $2.5/kg for 15 years. Similar to Germany's €3 billion hydrogen fund, India's ₹10,000 crore ($1.2 billion) supports alkaline and PEM electrolyzers. The policy encourages private investment in green ammonia and steel sectors.
learn.c3_text: Gujarat's Adani-Green Hydrogen project plans 1.5 GW capacity by 2026. Tamil Nadu's solar-powered electrolyzers will produce 100 tonnes/year. International partnerships with Japan and Australia aim for green ammonia exports. The mission aligns with India's 2070 net-zero target and renewable energy expansion.
learn.stat1: India's target: 5 MT green H2 by 2030
